property_summary: For any caller and any _unlockTime and deposit value, after calling Put the contract's recorded unlockTime for that caller is never less than block.timestamp (i.e., C ensures unlockTime >= now); the mutant that assigns unlockTime = _unlockTime can make it < now for some inputs, breaking this invariant.

For every call to Put by any actor with any _unlockTime and deposit, the contract records an unlockTime that is at least the current block.timestamp; the mutant that assigns unlockTime = _unlockTime can set it below now for some fuzzed _unlockTime, violating this invariant.

For any caller, if they call Put with any _unlockTime and send any nonzero ETH, then after Put returns the recorded unlockTime is >= the block.timestamp at which Put executed (the reference clamps to now; the mutant can set it earlier).

For every call to Put by any address with any _unlockTime and any deposit, if _unlockTime is in the future (strictly > block.timestamp) then after Put returns the recorded unlockTime equals the provided _unlockTime; the mutant that unconditionally assigns acc.unlockTime = _unlockTime can make the stored unlockTime be less than now for some inputs and thus violate this relation when _unlockTime > now is expected to be preserved.

For any caller and any provided _unlockTime and deposit, the reference contract never records an unlockTime earlier than the block timestamp after Put returns (it clamps to now); the mutant that assigns unlockTime = _unlockTime can set it below now for some inputs, violating this invariant.

For any caller and any _unlockTime and sent value, after Put the account's unlockTime is at least the block.timestamp passed at the call (i.e. acc.unlockTime >= block.timestamp); the mutant that always sets unlockTime = block.timestamp violates this when _unlockTime > block.timestamp because the reference stores the greater of _unlockTime and block.timestamp.

For any caller and any _unlockTime and sent value, after calling Put the stored unlockTime for that caller is >= the supplied _unlockTime (i.e., acc.unlockTime = max(_unlockTime, block.timestamp)); the mutant that forces acc.unlockTime = block.timestamp can make acc.unlockTime < _unlockTime when a caller supplies _unlockTime in the future.

For any caller and any _unlockTime and sent value, after a successful Put the stored unlockTime for that caller is at least the call-time block.timestamp OR equals the supplied _unlockTime when that supplied _unlockTime is in the future; the mutant that always writes block.timestamp can make the stored unlockTime strictly less than a supplied future _unlockTime, so the invariant that acc.unlockTime >= _unlockTime when _unlockTime > block.timestamp is violated by the mutant.

For any caller, when calling Put with a future _unlockTime (> block.timestamp), the contract stores acc.unlockTime equal to that future _unlockTime (i.e., acc.unlockTime >= block.timestamp and if _unlockTime > block.timestamp then acc.unlockTime == _unlockTime); the mutant that always sets acc.unlockTime = block.timestamp violates this by making stored unlockTime less than the provided future _unlockTime.

For any caller and any _unlockTime and payment, after calling Put the contract stores acc.unlockTime equal to max(_unlockTime, block.timestamp); the mutant that unconditionally sets acc.unlockTime = block.timestamp makes this false when _unlockTime > block.timestamp (i.e., stored unlockTime < supplied future _unlockTime).

For any caller and any msg.value, calling Put(...) on the correct contract never decreases the caller's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance (it either increases by msg.value or stays the same due to overflow prevention); the mutant that removes the overflow check can allow the stored balance to wrap and become smaller than before for some inputs, violating this invariant.

Invariant: calling Put(...) never decreases the stored Acc[caller].balance compared to its previous value (i.e. Acc[caller].balance_after >= Acc[caller].balance_before) for all inputs; the mutant removing the overflow require can cause an integer wrap so that balance_after < balance_before for some msg.value and prior balance.

For all inputs, calling Put(...) on the correct contract never makes the stored Acc[msg.sender].balance wrap-around and become less than it was before; removing the require allows wrap-around for some inputs so balance_after < balance_before.

For any caller and msg.value, calling Put(...) on the correct contract never makes the stored Acc[caller].balance overflow (i.e., Acc[caller].balance_after >= Acc[caller].balance_before); removing the require allows arithmetic wrap so for some inputs balance_after < balance_before.

For any caller and any msg.value, calling Put(...) never decreases that caller's stored Acc[caller].balance (i.e., Acc[caller].balance_after >= Acc[caller].balance_before) because the reference requires no overflow; the mutant removing the require can cause overflow/wrap and make the stored balance smaller for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonnegative payable amount, calling Put(...) on the correct contract increases (or leaves unchanged) that caller's recorded Acc balance by exactly msg.value (i.e., Acc[caller].balance_after == Acc[caller].balance_before + msg.value); the mutant rejects any nonzero msg.value (requires msg.value==0) and thus will revert for calls with msg.value>0, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonnegative msg.value, calling Put(...) on the reference contract never reverts and results in Acc[caller].balance increasing by msg.value (so a Put call with any value succeeds); the mutant requires msg.value==0 and therefore will revert for some inputs where msg.value>0, violating this rule.

For any caller and any nonnegative msg.value, after calling Put the contract's public Acc mapping reports that the caller's recorded balance is greater than or equal to the prior balance (i.e., Put never decreases the recorded balance); the mutant forbids any nonzero deposit (requires msg.value==0) and therefore either reverts for msg.value>0 or fails to increase the balance, violating this monotonic non-decrease property for some fuzzed msg.value.

For any caller and any nonnegative msg.value, calling Put(...) on the reference contract either accepts the deposit (succeeds) and makes the contract's balance increase by msg.value, or (if msg.value==0) succeeds with no balance change; the mutant rejects any nonzero msg.value (reverts), so there exist inputs (msg.value>0) where the reference succeeds but the mutant call reverts — we assert that a Put call with a fuzzed sender and fuzzed nonnegative value does NOT revert on the reference.

For any caller and any nonzero msg.value, calling Put(...) on the correct contract increases the contract's recorded Acc[caller].balance by msg.value and therefore makes address(c).balance increase by msg.value; the mutant requires msg.value==0 and will revert for some nonzero msg.value, so there exist fuzzed inputs (caller + positive value) where the reference succeeds and increases address(c).balance but the mutant call reverts — we assert that a Put call with a fuzzed sender and fuzzed positive value does NOT revert and increases address(c).balance accordingly.

After calling Put with a positive msg.value, the caller's Acc[msg.sender].balance increases by exactly msg.value (i.e., new balance >= previous balance and specifically equals previous+msg.value); the mutant resets acc.balance to zero breaking this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and any payable amount, after calling Put(...) the account balance stored in Acc for that caller is at least the sent msg.value (i.e., acc.balance >= msg.value); the mutant resets acc.balance to zero after Put, violating this for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero payable amount sent to Put, the account's stored Acc[caller].balance after successful Put must be at least the amount just sent (i.e., acc.balance >= msg.value); the mutant resets acc.balance to zero after Put, violating this for some inputs.

For any caller and any sent ETH amount, after calling Put(...) the contract's recorded Acc[caller].balance is at least as large as the previous stored balance (i.e., Put never decreases the stored balance); the mutant resets acc.balance to zero after adding msg.value, which can decrease balance and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any payable amount, after a successful Put the stored Acc[caller].unlockTime is set to at least the current block timestamp (i.e., unlockTime >= block.timestamp); the mutant still sets unlockTime but because acc.balance is zeroed it may allow later Collect behavior differences — however the direct invariant that Put sets unlockTime to >= block.timestamp holds in reference and the mutant also sets it, so instead we assert that after Put the contract's public Acc mapping reports the same unlockTime that was passed in (bounded to be >= block.timestamp) — the mutant will break this because zeroing balance does not change unlockTime, so we instead assert that after Put the caller's stored balance is equal to the contract's reported Acc balance decreased by zero?

For any caller and any deposit value, calling Put(x) increases that caller's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance by exactly msg.value (not more); the mutant doubles the increment for some inputs so this equality can be violated.

For any caller and any deposit amount, after calling Put(_unlockTime) the contract's recorded Acc[caller].balance increases by exactly the deposited msg.value (the mutant sometimes increases it by 2*msg.value, violating this equality).

For any depositor and any nonzero msg.value, a single call to Put increments the depositor's recorded Acc balance by at least msg.value (i.e. new_balance >= old_balance + msg.value); the mutant that adds msg.value twice can make the increment strictly greater than msg.value, violating the minimal increment rule for some input.

For every depositor and deposit amount, a single successful Put call increases that depositor's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance by exactly the deposited msg.value (i.e., newBalance - oldBalance == msg.value); the mutant that adds msg.value twice breaks this by sometimes making the increase equal 2*msg.value.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, after calling Put the contract's stored Acc[msg.sender].balance increases by either 0 (if msg.value==0) or by exactly msg.value; the mutant that adds msg.value twice can make the increase equal 2*msg.value for some fuzzed inputs, violating that equality.

After any successful Put by any sender with any nonnegative value, the reference contract records a log entry (increasing LogFile.History length / LastMsg) while the mutated version that removed the LogFile.AddMessage call does not; we assert that calling Put increases the log history length (so reference: always increases, mutant: for some inputs it will not).

For every Put call by any sender with any nonnegative msg.value, the reference implementation appends a Log.Message (increasing LogFile.History length and updating LastMsg), whereas the mutant that removed the AddMessage call does not always increase history length; thus after Put the History.length always increases in the reference but can stay the same in the mutant for some inputs.

For every call to Put by any sender that sends a nonzero value, the reference contract forwards that value plus sender info to the external Log contract by making an external call (which succeeds for a normal Log); the mutant that deleted the AddMessage call will NOT make that external call — so detectability: a Put that sends nonzero ETH causes the external Log contract's call count to increase in the reference but not in the mutant, which we observe by deploying a LoggingProbe that increments a counter when called.

For every call to Put by any sender (with any msg.value and unlock time), the reference implementation always makes an external call to its Log contract (so that a call to Put causes address(log).balance to reflect that external call did not transfer ETH but the Log contract's AddMessage is invoked), whereas the mutant that removed the AddMessage call does not invoke the external Log contract; we detect this by deploying a LoggingProbe that flips a public flag when AddMessage is invoked — the reference always sets the flag after Put, the mutant leaves it unset for some inputs.

For every call to Put by any sender, the correct contract always performs an external call to Log.AddMessage (so calling Put on c will not revert when the Log contract's fallback/receive reverts is handled by the caller), whereas the mutated contract that removed the logging call will differ in whether an external call occurs; we detect this by deploying a LoggingReverter that reverts when called — the reference will make the external call and thus the Put will revert (try/catch observes false) while the mutant (which removed the call) will succeed (try/catch observes true) for some fuzzed inputs.

For every call to Collect by an account, the reference contract only allows withdrawal when block.timestamp > acc.unlockTime (strictly after unlock); the mutant using >= permits withdrawal at block.timestamp == acc.unlockTime, which breaks this strict-timing invariant.

For every caller and inputs, the reference contract never allows Collect to succeed at exactly the stored unlockTime (it requires block.timestamp > unlockTime); the mutant (>=) can succeed when block.timestamp == unlockTime, violating that timing-strictness.

For every caller, amount and unlockTime, the reference contract never allows a successful Collect call at block.timestamp == stored unlockTime (it requires strictly greater); the mutant using '>=' can allow Collect to succeed when timestamp equals unlockTime, so there exists inputs where mutant succeeds but reference does not.

For any caller, amount and stored unlockTime, the reference contract never allows Collect to succeed when block.timestamp == acc.unlockTime (it requires block.timestamp > acc.unlockTime); the mutant using '>=' can allow Collect to succeed at timestamp == unlockTime, so there exist inputs where the mutant succeeds but the reference does not.

For all inputs, the reference contract C never allows a successful Collect(...) call when block.timestamp == acc.unlockTime (it requires block.timestamp > acc.unlockTime); the mutant changing the check to '>=' can allow a Collect to succeed at timestamp == unlockTime, so there exist inputs where mutant succeeds but reference does not.

For any caller, if their stored acc.balance is >= MinSum and they call Collect(_am) after unlockTime then the reference contract allows (succeeds) the transfer when _am <= acc.balance, whereas the mutant inverts the comparison and only allows calls when _am >= acc.balance — thus there exist inputs where reference succeeds but mutant rejects (or vice versa).

For any depositor and any amounts/times where the depositor has balance >= MinSum and unlockTime passed, calling Collect(_am) succeeds on the reference whenever _am <= balance; the mutant inverts the comparison (requires _am >= balance) and thus will make some such calls revert or not transfer — the test fuzzes actor, deposit amount, collect amount, and unlockTime to find a case where reference allows and mutant disallows.

For any actor, if they previously deposited >= MinSum and the unlockTime has passed, then calling Collect(_am) should succeed (transfer and reduce balance) whenever _am <= their recorded balance; the mutant inverts the comparison (requires _am >= balance) and thus will reject some such calls.

For any caller who previously deposited at least MinSum and whose unlockTime has passed, calling Collect(_am) succeeds (does not revert) on the reference whenever _am <= their recorded balance; the mutant inverts the comparison to require _am >= balance and therefore will reject some of these inputs.

For any caller who previously Put an amount >= MinSum and whose unlockTime has passed, calling Collect(_am) should succeed (not revert) on the reference whenever _am <= their recorded balance; the mutant inverts the comparison and will reject (revert) for some such inputs where 0 < _am < balance.

Reference C never allows a caller whose stored balance is below MinSum to successfully Collect any amount (the call will not send funds), while the mutant (which removed the MinSum check) can succeed for callers with balance < MinSum; the test fuzzes actor and amounts to find such a case.

For every caller and amount, if a caller's stored balance is strictly less than MinSum then calling Collect must NOT transfer funds (balance remains unchanged / call does not succeed in sending value); the mutant that removed the MinSum check allows Collect to succeed for callers whose stored balance < MinSum for some inputs.

For any caller and amount, if the caller's stored balance is strictly less than MinSum then calling Collect must never transfer Ether (the Collect call either does nothing or reverts); the mutant removing the MinSum check allows a Collect to succeed (transfer funds) for some caller whose stored balance < MinSum.
